questions.qtext:
Consider the language of the Acceptance Problem for Turing Machines:

$$
A_{T M}=\{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text { is a TM and } w \text { is in } L(M)\}
$$
Define a Turing Machine $N$ with the following behavior:

$N=$ "On input $\langle M, w\rangle$ :

1. Simulate $M$ on input $w$.

2. If $M$ accepts, accept. If $M$ rejects, reject."

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE regarding the Turing Machine $N$ ?

options.text: $N$ always halts on any given valid input $\langle M, w\rangle$

questions.solution:
Answer: B, A

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Answer: $\text{B}$ only.

$N$ recognizes $A_{TM}$ because:

  • If $\langle M, w \rangle \in A_{TM}$, then $M$ accepts $w$ and $N$ accepts.
  • If $\langle M, w \rangle \notin A_{TM}$, $M$ either rejects (so $N$ rejects) or loops forever (so $N$ does not halt).

Hence, $N$ semi-decides $A_{TM}$, but does not decide it.

  • $\text{A}$ is false: $A_{TM}$ is undecidable.
  • $\text{C}$ is false: $M$ may loop on $w$, so $N$ may not halt.
  • $\text{D}$ is false: $N$ recognizes $A_{TM}$. So, how it can decide complement of $A_{TM} ?$ Also, $\overline{A_{TM}}$ is undecidable.

options.text: Given two Turing machines $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$, decide if $L \left(M_{1} \right) = L \left(M_{2}\right)$.
Given a Turing machine $M$, decide if $L(M)$ is regular.
Given a Turing machine $M$, decide if $M$ accepts all strings.
Given a Turing machine $M$, decide if $M$ takes more than $1073$ steps on every string.

questions.solution:
Answer: D, A

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Answer : D

$L_4 = \{ \langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ is a Turing Machine and} \,\, M \text{ takes more than } 1073 \text{ steps on every string} \} $

$L_4$ is decidable as we can have a systematic procedure (algorithm, which terminates in some finite amount of time for every input) in deciding whether a given Turing machine $M$ takes more than $1073$ steps on every string.

For $L_4$ we have to monitor for at most $\textsf{TM}$ for $1073+1$ steps for all possible inputs of size $<=1073$ (if the input set is having $k$ alphabets, we will have finite number of such possible strings which we need to inspect on the input Turing Machine.) Let’s call all these strings of length $<=1073$ as the “candidate strings” (candidates for inspection on the input TM)(So, we have finite number of candidate strings)

Our algorithm takes Turing Machine as input.

If for all the candidate strings, Input Turing Machine $M$ is taking more than $1073$ steps, then it means for all larger strings(strings of length $>1073$) also $M$ must take more than $1073$ steps and we(our algorithm) can answer “yes” for input $M.$

If for at least one of the candidate strings, Input Turing Machine $M$ is halting in less than or equal to $1073$ steps, then we(our algorithm) can answer “No” for input $M.$

So, we can decide, for any input Turing machine $M,$ whether $M$ takes more than 1073 steps on every string Or whether $M$ halts in less than or equal to 1073 steps on at least one string.

Thus we(our algorithm) correctly decided $L_4.$

So, Problem in Option D is Decidable.

NOTE :

For Option D, we cannot apply Rice Theorem as the property mentioned in the Problem of Option D, is about the Turing machine and not about the language. Rice Theorem is applicable only for the languages of Turing Machines.

$L_1 :$

Option 1 is the “Equivalence Problem of Turing Machines” which asks to Decide whether two TMs accept the same language. This is equivalent to the problem of whether two programs compute the same output for every input. This is standard undecidable problem.

Though, we cannot apply Rice Theorem for $L_1$ as Rice Theorem is applicable only when input is a single Turing Machine and the problem to be decided is related to language of this Turing Machine.

$L_2 :$

Option 2 is the “Regularity Problem of Turing Machines” which asks to Decide whether the language accepted by the given TM is a regular language. This is standard undecidable problem. We can also apply Rice Theorem for $L_2$. $L_2$ is undecidable using Rice Theorem because “language of Turing machine” being Regular is Non-trivial property of “languages of TM”. In simple terms, language of TMs is RE language and “being regular” is Non-Trivial Property of RE languages. As per Rice Theorem, ALL Non-trivial properties of RE languages are Undecidable.

Examples of undecidable problems :
• About Turing machines:
– Is the language accepted by a TM empty, finite, regular, or context-free?
– Does a TM meet its “specification,” that is, does it have any “bugs.”
• About context-free languages:
– Are two context-free grammars equivalent?
– Is a context-free grammar ambiguous?

$L_3 :$

Option 3 is the “Universaility/Completeness Problem of Turing Machines” which asks to Decide whether the TM accepts all strings or not. This is standard undecidable problem. We can also apply Rice Theorem for $L_3$. $L_3$ is undecidable using Rice Theorem because “language of Turing machine” being $\Sigma^*$ is Non-trivial property of “languages of TM”. In simple terms, language of TMs is RE language and “being $\Sigma^*$” is Non-Trivial Property of RE languages. As per Rice Theorem, ALL Non-trivial properties of RE languages are Undecidable

questions.qtext:
Define languages $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ as follows :

$L_{1} =\{\langle M, w, 0 \rangle \mid M$ accepts $w\}$

$L_{2} =\{\langle M, w, 1 \rangle \mid M$ does not accept $w\}$

Here $\langle M,w,i \rangle $ is a triplet, whose first component $M$ is an encoding of a Turing Machine, second component $w$ is a string, and third component $i$ is a bit.

Let $L = L_{1} \cup L_{2}$. Which of the following is/are false?

options.text: $L_{1}$ is recursively enumerable but $L_2$ is not

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Answer: $ oxed{ extbf{A, B}}$

Most common mistake it to think $L_1 = A_{TM}$ and $L_2 = \overline{A_{TM}}$, where $A_{TM}$ is Acceptance Problem for TMs.

First understand language $L_1$ and language $L_2$.

For the sake of example, consider three Turing Machines: $A$, $B$ and $C$ and input string $w \in \Sigma^*$. Suppose, $A$ accepts $w$, $B$ rejects $w$ and $C$ loops on $w$. Now,

$L_{1} =\{\langle M, w, 0 angle \mid M$ accepts $w\}$

  • $\langle A, w, 0 angle \in L_1$ because $A$ accepts $w$.
  • $\langle B, w, 0 angle otin L_1$ because $B$ does not accept $w$.
  • $\langle C, w, 0 angle otin L_1$ because $C$ does not accept $w$.

So, if someone gives you triplet: $\langle M, w, 0 angle$ and tells you that it belongs to $L_1$ then it means TM $M$ accepts $w$. And if someone tells you that it doesn't belong to $L_1$, then it means TM $M$ doesn't accept $w$.

$L_{2} =\{\langle M, w, 1 angle \mid M$ does not accept $w\}$. Similarly,

  • $\langle A, w, 1 angle otin L_2$ because $A$ accepts $w$.
  • $\langle B, w, 1 angle \in L_2$ because $B$ does not accept $w$.
  • $\langle C, w, 1 angle \in L_2$ because $C$ does not accept $w$.

$L_1$ is RE. We can simulate $M$ on $w$. If $M$ accepts, accept and if $M$ rejects, reject. But $L_2$ is not recursively enumerable. Option $\color{red}{ oxed{C}}$ is correct.

It is given that $L = L_1 \cup L_2$.

It should be noted that every string in $L_1, L_2$ and $L$ are in the form of triplet. In particular, members of $L_1$ are of the form $\langle M, w, 0 angle$, members of $L_2$ are of the form $\langle M, w, 1 angle$ and members of $L$ are of the form $\langle M, w, i angle$ where $i$ can be $0$ or $1$.

So, if someone tells you that the triplet $\langle M, w, 0 angle \in L$ then it must have came from $L_1$ since every triplet that is in $L_1$ has $0$ in the third component and every triplet that is in $L_2$ does not have $0$ in the third component. And since $\langle M, w, 0 angle \in L_1$, $M$ accepts $w$.

In that same way, if someone tells you that the triplet $\langle M, w, 1 angle \in L$ then it must have came from $L_2$ since every triplet that is in $L_2$ has $1$ in the third component and every triplet that is in $L_1$ does not have $1$ in the third component. And since $\langle M, w, 1 angle \in L_2$, $M$ does not accept $w$.

So,

  • $\color{blue}{\langle M, w, 0 angle \in L} \iff \langle M, w, 0 angle \in L_1 \iff$ $\color{blue}{ ext{M accepts w}}$
  • $\color{blue}{\langle M, w, 1 angle \in L} \iff \langle M, w, 1 angle \in L_2 \iff$ $\color{blue}{ ext{M does not accept w}}$

One another mistake is to consider $L = \Sigma^*$. But it is not so since not every string belongs to $L$.
We know that, for every Turing Machine $M$ and for every input string $w$, either $M$ accepts $w$ or does not accept.
If $M$ accepts $w$, then $\langle M, w, 1 angle otin L$ and $\langle M, w, 0 angle \in L$
If $M$ does not accept $w$, then $\langle M, w, 0 angle otin L$ and $\langle M, w, 1 angle \in L$
So clearly, $L eq \Sigma^*$. Option $\color{red}{ oxed{A}}$ is incorrect.

$L$ is not RE.

If $L$ were RE, then we could decide the Acceptance Problem of TMs:
Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that $L$ is RE. Then there exists a TM $T$ that recognizes $L$.

On input $\langle M,w angle$:

  • Construct strings: $\langle M, w, 0 angle$ and $\langle M, w, 1 angle$
  • Simulate $T$ on both of these strings in dovetailing fashion.
  • Since exactly one of the two simulations must eventually accept.
  • If $T$ accepts $\langle M,w,0 angle$, $ extbf{halt and accept}$
  • Otherwise, if $T$ accepts $\langle M,w,1 angle$, $ extbf{halt and reject}$

Thus, we have constructed a decider for ${A}_{TM}$, which is impossible. Hence, $L$ is not RE. Option $\color{red}{ oxed{B}}$ is incorrect.

Another Proof: Let $X$ denotes the set of all strings of the form $\langle M,w,1 angle$, i.e., all valid encodings whose third component is $1$. If $L$ were RE, then $L_2 = L \cap X$ would also be RE, since RE langauges are closed under intersection. But $L_2$ is not RE. Therefore, $L$ is not RE. ($X$ is RE because we just need to check if string is valid encoding or not.)

Now, what is $\overline{L} ?$

We have seen above that, for every TM $M$ and for every input string $w$, exactly one of $\langle M, w, 0 angle$ and $\langle M, w, 1 angle$ belongs to $L$. So, this is also the case with $\overline{L}$ that exactly one of those two triplets belongs to $\overline{L}$.

\[
L=
\left\{
\langle M,w,i angle
\;\middle|\;
(i=0 \land M ext{ accepts } w)
\;\lor\;
(i=1 \land M ext{ does not accept } w)
ight\}
\]

If we assume $\Sigma^*$ is set of all valid encodings, then

\[
\overline{L}=
\left\{
\langle M,w,i angle
\;\middle|\;
(i=1 \land M ext{ accepts } w)
\;\lor\;
(i=0 \land M ext{ does not accept } w)
ight\}
\]

If there can be invalid encodings, then

\[
egin{aligned}
\overline{L}
={}&
\left(
\Sigma^*
\setminus
\left\{
\langle M,w,i angle
\mid
M ext{ is an encoding of a TM},\;
w\in\Sigma^*,\;
i\in\{0,1\}
ight\}
ight) \
&\cup
\left\{
\langle M,w,i angle
\;\middle|\;
(i=1 \land M ext{ accepts } w)
\;\lor\;
(i=0 \land M ext{ does not accept } w)
ight\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

(Note: LHS of union is just set of all invalid encodings. $\langle M, w angle$, $\langle M angle$, $\epsilon$, etc are invalid encodings/format)

Observe that $L$ and $\overline{L}$ are symmetric. The only difference is the interpretation of the indicator bit $i$, which is reversed. So, $\overline{L}$ is also not RE. (Same reason as why $L$ is not RE). So, option $\color{red}{ oxed{D}}$ is correct.
